name: Campa
confidence_why: Dirks 1953 (as quoted in Crothers, Lorentz, Sherman & Vihman 1979) reports one stress per word that tends to the penult with unexplained exceptions and is probably phonemic, whereas Pike & Kindberg 1956, the only study devoted to Campa stress, describe up to five primary stresses per word whose distribution behaves like high tone, a system Goedemans, Heinz & van der Hulst 2015 could only encode as no metrical stress and Hyman 1977 proposed reanalysing with secondary stresses, so the two first-hand descriptions agree only that stress is not rule-governed and no later work on Asháninka settles what kind of system it is.

Lorentz, Donald A. Sherman & Marilyn M. Vihman (eds.). 1979. catalog_locator: Dirks 1953: 303 (§2, stress paragraph) and 302 (§1.1, post-nasal voicing), as carried in SPA Handbook 1979: 479, field '$a STRESS' and footnote 925 60.

(p. 303) [...] 925 60 $A The stops (but not the affricates) are voiced after nasals. "However, in the second syllable of dissyllabic words in which stress falls on the first syllable this variation does not occur," (p. 302)
sweep_summary: asha1243 (Asháninka, Kampa/Arawakan) is not in the catalog. this search of works with stress in the title's single title-keyword item, Crowhurst & Michael 2005 (Language 81), is about Nanti (nant1250), not Asháninka: read in full from the author's self-archived copy already held by the project (copied to asha1243/); its only Kampa comparison is one clause citing Payne 1990 for Ashéninka as a typical iambic language, so it is a Glottolog mis-link for this languoid and irrelevant to Asháninka stress. No first-hand statement of Asháninka-proper word stress could be read: Pike & Kindberg 1956 (Río Apurímac Campa, Word 12; nominally open at T&F but 403 to every scripted download, no the Internet Archive/archive.org copy) and Dirks 1953 (IJAL 19; uchicago/JSTOR blocked) remain unread, high priority; Payne 1990/1991 (Ashéninka, other variety) not located, medium. The only stress statement held by the project for this language is the second-hand Dirks 1953:303 quotation in the Stanford Phonology Archive handbook (penult tendency with numerous exceptions, possibly phonemic). discovery used Crossref, Unpaywall, OpenAlex, S2, archive.org and direct URLs.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (3 pp., PHOIBLE upload of SPA Handbook entry 925 Campa) opened; page 2 of the PDF = Handbook p. 479 re-rendered to PNG and read on the scan image. The field reads exactly: "$a STRESS $A "Stress tends to fall on the penult but thus far no rule has been found to account for the numerous exceptions.. Stress will probably prove to be phonemic." (p.303)" — verbatim as reported (the compilers "(p. 303)" vs the scan's "(p.303)" is only spacing). Footnote 60 on the same page also verified: "The stops (but not the affricates) are voiced after nasals. "However, in the second syllable of dissyllabic words in which stress falls on the first syllable this variation does not occur." (p.302)". Header…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress usually falls on the penultimate syllable, but there are many exceptions for which no rule was found, and the author expects stress to turn out to be contrastive (lexically distinctive). A related remark (Dirks p. 302, also quoted in the SPA entry) implies that some disyllables carry stress on the first syllable, i.e. penultimate, while others do not.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in the quoted material. The title of Pike & Kindberg 1956 ('A problem in multiple stresses', on the Apurímac Asháninka) indicates that several degrees of stress were later recognised, but that article could not be opened.
new_statements.exceptions: 'Numerous exceptions' to the penult tendency; no rule found for them.
new_statements.domain_note: Word level; based on six months with a single informant (SPA header: '$q informant $r six months'). Tentative 1953 phonemic sketch; no modern first-hand description of asháninka-proper stress could be opened.
new_statements.identity_note: The only stress statement found is Dirks 1953 on 'Campa', which Montoya 2021:26 identifies as the asháninka of the Río Tambo (asha1243); Pike & Kindberg 1956 concern the Río Apurímac asháninka (also asha1243). The stress rules summarised in Martel 2012 (from J. Payne 1990/1991) and the 'Normas de acentuación' held under ajyi1238 (Payne 1980) describe Ashéninka varieties (Alto Perené ashe1273 area / Apurucayali ajyi1238), not asha1243.

new_statements.quote: In the Campa language of Eastern Peru, a single grammatically defined word may have as many as three, four, or five primary stresses, with frequently three, and occasionally as many as four primary stresses on contiguous phonemic syllables of a word. Phonetically the persistent, significant contrasts are of stress, but distributionally the placement of stress acts much like a high tone. (Pike & Kindberg 1956:415-416) [passage 765] || Campa appears to have a stress system in which stress has the distribution of tone. ... It may be encoded as a NMS system, because all stresses appear to be of equal intensity. ... However, Pike & Kindberg clearly state that all stresses are primary. [note 755, Remarks, PJK]

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Note 755 is verbatim in the saved static page (tag-stripped: 'Remarks : Campa appears to have a stress system in which stress has the distribution of tone. Still, Campa does not appear to be a pitch accent language, because pitch varies even though stress remains stable. It is therefore very hard to classify this system. It may be encoded as a NMS system, because all stresses appear to be of equal intensity. Hyman (1977: 69) wonders.. However, Pike & Kindberg clearly state that all stresses are primary.. PJK'), together with 'Affix_comm : Affixes may be inherently stressed, cause stress on another morpheme or delete stress', the pattern rows 'Exceptional (Campa)' and 'in_toto In progress',…
new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the existing Dirks 1953 statement that stress is phonemic/unpredictable ('Stress will probably prove to be phonemic'), but describes a different type of system: Dirks implies one stress per word tending to the penult with many exceptions, whereas Pike & Kindberg (via StressTyp2) describe several primary stresses per word with no culminative stress and a tone-like distribution. Identity caveat: the database maps this lect to cjo (Pajonal Ashéninka) on its own guess; Montoya 2021: 26 places Pike & Kindberg's data on the Río Apurímac (asha1243). StressTyp2 also miscredits the article to 'E.V. Pike'; the author is Kenneth L. Pike.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Second-hand from Pike & Kindberg 1956: word stress is phonemic (contrastive) and non-culminative; a word may carry up to five primary stresses, often on adjacent syllables, distributed like a high tone; no placement rule. StressTyp2 itself says the system is 'very hard to classify' and encodes it as NMS (no metrical stress), with the lect's affixes noted as inherently stressed / stress-attracting / stress-deleting.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Pattern 'secondary: No information'. Note 755 reports Hyman (1977: 69) wondering whether some of the stresses could be reanalysed as secondary or echo stresses, but records that Pike & Kindberg call all of them primary.
new_statements.exceptions: A pattern row 'Exceptional (Campa)' exists with no content; Affix_comm: 'Affixes may be inherently stressed, cause stress on another morpheme or delete stress.'
new_statements.identity_note: Vilchez 2004 targets the Tambo-Ene variety (asha1243 proper; she calls it the most conservative). Adam 1890 edits an 18th-century Franciscan Arte of the 'Antis o Campas' of the Sonomoro, San Antonio, Ene and Perené missions and Cerro de la Sal, with remarks on Chabini/Pajonal pronunciation differences; it predates the modern Asháninka/Ashéninka split. the StressTyp2 entry for this language is mapped by the database to Pajonal Ashéninka (ISO cjo), but the underlying Pike & Kindberg 1956 data are reported by Montoya 2021: 26 to be Río Apurímac Asháninka (asha1243).

new_statements.quote: (p. 415) In the Campa language of Eastern Peru a single grammatically defined word may have as many as three, four, or five primary stresses, with frequently three and, occasionally, as many as four primary stresses on contiguous phonemic syllables of a word. (p. 416) [...] no minimal pairs have yet been found for pitch or stress by either of the authors, even though the presence of phonemic stress is certain because of sharp pattern contrasts and because of abundant contrasts in analogous environment. (p. 421) [...] phonemic stresses must be certainly postulated, with pitch nonphonemic [...] Sequences of three stresses contrast with sequences of two; two stresses contrast with one
new_statements.citation: Pike, Kenneth L. & Willard Kindberg. 1956. A problem in multiple stresses. Word 12(3): 415-428.
new_statements.locator: Pike & Kindberg 1956: 415-416 (section 0 Introduction) and 421 (section 6 'Multiple stress phonemes on long words') = pp. 63, 64, 69 of; same lines in lines ~44-71 and ~510-519).
new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's classification (lexical, from Dirks 1953 via SPA 1979: 'Stress will probably prove to be phonemic') and makes it first-hand and stronger: Pike & Kindberg state outright that stress is phonemic/contrastive and add what Dirks lacks - several contrastive primary stresses per word (number and contiguity contrastive), pitch nonphonemic, and suffix-driven morphophonemic stress loss/addition. It does NOT support Dirks's 'tends to fall on the penult' as a default (no positional tendency is proposed; stem-stress and rhythm hypotheses were tried and rejected), and it is a different dialect (Mantaro/Apurimac vs Dirks's lower Tambo, p. 415, fn. 7), so the penult-tendency h…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress in (Mantaro/Apurimac) Campa is phonemic: it cannot be predicted from position, there are no minimal pairs yet but abundant contrasts in analogous environments, and a single grammatical word regularly carries several primary stresses (often three, up to four or five, sometimes on adjacent syllables); the number and the contiguity of stresses are themselves contrastive. Pitch is not phonemic: it is partly conditioned by stress and segmental shape and partly free, which is why the system first looked tonal ('distributionally the placement of stress acts much like a high tone', p. 416). Stress placement is lexical per morpheme and adjusted by morphophonemic rules under suffixation. No default position (penult or other) is proposed; the authors explicitly abandoned stem-stress and rhythm-unit hypotheses (sections 3-4).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None distinguished: the article recognises only one degree, 'primary stress', of which a word may carry several (p. 415 'as many as three, four, or five primary stresses'); it also notes nonphonemic half-length and optional pitch glides on stressed vowels (p. 421) and long words of 6-12 moras breaking into two or more rhythm units (p. 419, 421).
new_statements.exceptions: Morphophonemic stress alternations (p. 421-422): 'a three-syllable three-stress stem loses its final stress when it precedes, without juncture, the stressed suffix -pé plural indicator'; 'Other suffixes carry with them a pre-suffixal stress, as does -niré bad' (pócoti.haniki 'small achote' vs pocotíniré 'bad achote'); two-syllable stems mááná, ¢éiité, kiimá 'lost their last stress' before -bé 'many' / -pé 'plural', and méiri 'gained a stem-final stress in méiriniro' (p. 422-423). Also: utterance-final syllables (sometimes the last two) optionally devoice, concealing stem-final stress and pitch (pp. 422, 426); CVV counts as two phonemic syllables/moras for stress patterning (p. 419). Dialect caveat: the data are Mantaro/Apurimac Ashaninka, said to differ 'considerably' from Gran Pajonal and less from Dirks's lower Tambo (p. 415).
new_statements.identity_note: Pike & Kindberg 1956 treats 'Campa' of eastern Peru from Willard Kindberg's SIL field data; SIL archive entry 30125 tags it Ashaninka [cni] = asha1243 and Montoya 2021: 26 places the data on the Rio Apurimac (asha1243), whereas StressTyp2/WALS attach the same article to Pajonal Asheninka (cjo, ashe1273). Not verifiable from the text (no copy).

readall_conflicts: The two descriptive statements available for 'Campa' disagree in type though not in predictability. Dirks 1953: 303 (second-hand in the SPA Handbook 1979: 479, already in the catalog) implies one stress per word that 'tends to fall on the penult' with 'numerous exceptions' and 'will probably prove to be phonemic'. Pike & Kindberg 1956: 415-416, read here only second-hand through the StressTyp2 entry(and Hyman 1977: 38, 69 n.5 already held by the project), describe a non-culminative system with up to five primary stresses per word whose distribution 'acts much like a high tone'; StressTyp2 encodes it as NMS and calls it 'very hard to classify', and Hyman suggests an echo/secondary-stress reanalysis. Whether this is a real disagreement or two varieties is open: StressTyp2 files the Pike & Kindberg lect under Pajonal Ashéninka (cjo) by its own guess, while Montoya 2021: 26 places their data on the Río Apurímac (asha1243). The two works newly opened in full (Vilchez 2004; Adam 1890) say nothing about stress, and Pike & Kindberg 1956 itself remains unread (tandfonline 403).

tone.quote: The basic prosodic unit is the prosodic word (PW), which is the domain of stress assignment. The prosodic word is isomorphic with a phonological word (prosodic units form phonological domains). The stress system shows weight sensitivity. The heavy syllables CVV, CVN, and CVVN generally attract stress. Overall, Satipo Ashaninka is a stress accent iambic language (with the weak-strong and right headed iamb). The primary metrical stress is associated with an increase in duration and fundamental frequency and intensity. [...] The left edge boundary tone usually carries strong pitch prominence. The demarcative function of the left edge boundary tone is also manifest in the genetically related and geographically adjacent Alto Perené (Kampa Arawak) in [15].
tone.locator: p. 25, §1 Introduction (right column); phrasal Hp and boundary tones L%/H% at pp. 25-26 §1-2
tone.summary: No lexical tone: stress-accent language (weight-sensitive iambic stress cued by duration, F0 and intensity); H and L tones exist only as intonational events (phrase-final Hp, left-edge boundary tone, utterance-final L%/H%) - stated for Satipo Ashaninka, with the left-edge boundary tone said to hold for Alto Perené too.
